text:
- chief complaint: post-traumatic right index finger pain, swelling, and stiffness following a motor vehicle accident in March, with inability to make a fist and pain with driving.
- history of present illness: the patient was a passenger in a rear-ended car and felt the right index finger hyperextended. Pain and swelling have persisted since then despite orthopedic care, occupational therapy, and MRI showing a partial-thickness tear of the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) with tenosynovitis. The patient was previously denied injection due to the tear, and has had a prior steroid reaction (dexamethasone and methylprednisolone).
- physical examination: no acute distress; 2+ radial pulse; no visible bruising or swelling; diminished sensation over the PIP joint; index finger rests in 10-degree PIP flexion; pain with active flexion and passive stretching; limited fist formation.
- symptoms experienced by the patient: pain, swelling, stiffness, numbness, inability to make a fist, pain with driving.
- new medications prescribed or changed, including dosages: betamethasone (Celestone) 1 cc steroid injection into the right index flexor tendon sheath with 0.5 cc lidocaine; ibuprofen recommended for pain (dosage N/A).
- follow-up instructions: outpatient physical therapy once a week for six weeks, with the goal of full active and passive range of motion; icing the finger the evening of the procedure; accountability check-ins with the therapist weekly; the patient may drive.
